newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lebed tells NATO tread carefully on expansion.
newsitem.headline: Lebed tells NATO tread carefully on expansion.

text.p: Russia's outspoken security chief Alexander Lebed on Monday entered what for two decades of his army career was the enemy "Lion's Den" and emerged cautioning NATO against any hasty expansion eastwards.

The ex-paratroop general with burning presidential ambitions said after talks at NATO headquarters he had heard no new ideas from Secretary-General Javier Solana on plans Lebed sees as a threat to Russia. The alliance, he said, must work with Russia.
"Every step must be calculated," he said, booming out the sylables in a voice made for the parade ground.
"Take stock, take stock and take stock again."

But, speaking to reporters in warm sunshine on his first Western visit, he proposed an arrangement that would spare Moscow what would be the demeaning prospect of NATO riding rough-shod over Russian objections.

"I came to say let's work together, let's solve the problem...of modernising, reforming NATO, the establishment of special, as we say, relations between Russia and NATO, expressed in an agreement or treaty with legal status and then, further, take a decision on expansion or non-expansion," he said.
The comments contrasted starkly with a past description of NATO behaving like a drunken hooligan in a kindergarten over its plans to incorporate former Warsaw Pact members.
A senior NATO official said Solana had rejected any idea of a link between a treaty and expansion. But he said Lebed appeared to accept the notion that expansion was inevitable.
He described Lebed as a highly intelligent man in a rational "listening mode". There was, he said, no "over the top language".
"We are enormously encouraged...We see him as a very important figure whatever the future holds," the official said.

Lebed, sporting a crisp civilian suit but his military bearing intact, had brushed aside official entreaties to step into a limousine and strode up to journalists waiting at a gate. He is a military man with fast-developing political instincts.

Western officials are eager to gain a first-hand impression of the man who performed so strongly in the election earlier this year. If Boris Yeltsin fails to return to his duties after heart surgery scheduled this year, he would be a strong candidate to succeed.

The NATO headquarters, a rambling, fenced complex of low brick buildings, was the object of scorn in Cold War Soviet media, described variously as a "nest of vipers" and "Lion's Den". Lebed says that, while he has disavowed communism, it is NATO that has failed to adapt to the post-Cold War era.

Lebed is an unknown quantity to the West, familiar largely through his extraordinary voice. For many officials here and in NATO capitals he has the same "maverick" aura as Boris Yeltsin had in the years before he edged Mikhail Gorbachev from power.
His comments, rich in imagery, are as colourful as they are sometimes contradictory.

These days the ailing Yeltsin is seen as guardian of continuity. The uncertainty surrounds Lebed. A political newcomer he may be, but he demonstrated diplomatic skill in defusing ethnic conflict in Moldova when 14th Army commander and acted decisively in forging a peace in breakaway Chechnya.
Lebed said he had had no time to put his own new proposals to Solana on the expansion plans. These, he said, would be presented later on Monday at a meeting with NATO ambassadors.

In an article on Monday for the English-language International Herald Tribune, Solana proposed that Russia and NATO station permanent liasion officers in their respective military commands to help build a closer relationship.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry proposed last month that the alliance "throw open its doors" to Russia to help convince Moscow its intentions were not hostile.

Lebed has said on many occasions he would like to take Russia's fate into his own hands as president. Among his priorities would be increased funding for the forces which he said recently are on the verge of mutiny because spending cuts.
On Tuesday he is scheduled to visit NATO's military command headquarters in the town of Mons, centre of operations for alliance forces in Bosnia.
